analysis.investment_thesis: MIDHANI is a strategic defence PSU with a near-monopoly in super alloys/titanium for Indian aerospace and defence, but it violates virtually every SMILE criterion — market cap of ₹6,938 Cr is 7x my upper limit, P/E at 63x is 4-5x my comfort zone, and net profit has shrunk at -2.7% CAGR over 6 years. At this price, defence indigenisation tailwinds are already more than priced in.
key_strengths: Near-monopoly supplier of super alloys, titanium, and specialty steels for Indian defence/aerospace — irreplaceable strategic asset
FCF finally turning positive (₹136 Cr in FY24, ₹149 Cr in FY25) as the heavy capex/CWIP cycle (₹405 Cr → ₹24 Cr) completes
Debt/Equity at a manageable 0.23 with 74% government promoter holding providing stability
key_risks: Catastrophic valuation mismatch — P/E 63x on a business with -2.7% net profit CAGR over 6 years and only 7.1% revenue CAGR; zero margin of safety
PSU bureaucracy suppresses entrepreneurial drive: government-controlled management with no 'large aspiration' culture; growth is policy-dependent, not vision-driven
Profitability structurally deteriorating — operating income contracted, ROE collapsed to 8.1%, finance costs compounding at 27.4% CAGR eating into slim gains
red_flags: Market cap ₹6,938 Cr — 7x outside my ₹100–1,000 Cr SMILE sweet spot; institutional investors have already 'discovered' this
P/E of 63x (Forward 38.5x) on a PSU with declining net profit — this is a speculative defence theme bet, not a value entry
Net profit fell from ₹177 Cr (FY22) to ₹92 Cr (FY24), recovering only to ₹111 Cr in FY25 — a ₹711 Cr revenue base in 2019 has only reached ₹1,074 Cr in 2025, barely 1.5x in six years
ROE 8.1% and ROCE 10.6% — destroying value relative to cost of capital; no operational leverage visible despite scale
analysis.detailed_analysis:
MIDHANI is a 50-year-old government PSU with genuine strategic importance — India simply cannot afford to import super alloys and titanium for its DRDO/ISRO/Navy programmes. That moat is real. But strategic importance does not equal investment opportunity. Revenue has crawled from ₹711 Cr to ₹1,074 Cr over six years (7.1% CAGR), net profit has actually shrunk (-2.7% CAGR), and the stock market has priced all the Atmanirbhar Bharat optimism into a 63x P/E multiple. The company is not in early stages of expansion — it is a mature, slow-growing monopolist inside a captive government supply chain.

From my SMILE lens, this fails on every dimension that matters. 'S' — too large at ₹6,938 Cr. 'M' — PSU management, not hungry entrepreneurs. 'L' — no 5-10x aspiration, growth is budgetary. 'E' — TAM is large in defence, but MIDHANI's addressable share is narrow and government-rationed. The only silver lining is that the capex cycle has ended (CWIP at ₹24 Cr vs ₹405 Cr in FY20), and FCF is now positive at ~₹149 Cr, suggesting some earnings recovery ahead. But even if profits double to ₹220 Cr, you're paying 31x on that — still not a Kedia price. Wait for a significant correction to sub-₹150 or find better SMILE candidates elsewhere in the defence supply chain at smaller market caps.
